steps.title: Key to bucket
steps.caption: Each key's hash mod 8 picks its bucket; get(bob) repeats the same math and goes straight there.
steps.body: Each `put` runs the key through a hash function (32-bit FNV-1a here) and reduces the hash to a bucket index with `hash mod 8`: alice hashes to `0x872213E7` and lands in bucket 7, bob in 4 and carol in 2. A `get` repeats the same calculation and goes straight to that bucket, so on average it costs the same however many entries the table holds: **O(1)**.

steps.title: Collisions share a bucket
steps.caption: dave also lands in bucket 7, so that bucket keeps a chain; get(dave) compares keys along it.
steps.body: dave hashes to `0xD06CC5DF`, which also gives bucket 7, so the bucket keeps a short **chain** (separate chaining): alice, then dave. `get(dave)` goes to bucket 7 and compares keys along the chain: alice is not equal, dave is, and it returns 38. A shared bucket, or even an identical hash, does not mean the keys are equal, so the key comparison is always needed.

steps.title: Grow before it clogs
steps.caption: grace makes 7 entries in 8 buckets, over 0.75, so the table doubles to 16 and rehashes every entry.
steps.body: erin and frank bring the table to 6 entries in 8 buckets, a **load factor** of 0.75. grace collides with frank in bucket 3 and makes 7, more than 0.75 × 8 = 6, so the table doubles to 16 buckets and rehashes every entry with `mod 16`: alice, bob, carol and frank stay where they are, while erin moves to 9, grace to 11 and dave to 15. The load factor drops to 7/16 ≈ 0.44. A resize copies everything (O(n)), but doubling makes it rare enough that inserts stay **O(1) amortized**.

steps.title: When hashing goes wrong
steps.caption: Five keys built to share one hash all chain in bucket 5, so a lookup there scans them all: O(n).
steps.body: FNV-1a has no secret, so colliding keys can be computed offline: these five 5-character keys all hash to `0x91AB64A5` and pile into bucket 5 while the load factor stays within its 0.75 limit. A lookup there scans the chain (5 compares for the last key, n in general), and inserting n such keys costs O(n²) compares: **hash flooding**, demonstrated against many web platforms in December 2011. The defences are keyed hashes with a random seed (SipHash), Java's tree bins and limits on request size.
